content.title: Evaluating New Evidence for Conflicting Viewpoints
content.overview: In the ACT Science section, you will often encounter 'Conflicting Viewpoints' passages where two or more scientists or models offer different explanations for a phenomenon. This lesson teaches you how to determine which viewpoint a new piece of evidence supports by matching predictions to results and verifying experimental controls.
learning_objectives: Identify the specific predictions made by competing scientific viewpoints.
Compare new experimental data to predictions based on direction and magnitude.
Evaluate whether experimental controls effectively rule out alternative explanations.
Determine which viewpoint is best supported by a given set of new results.

sections.title: The Prediction-Match Strategy
sections.content: When presented with new evidence, your first task is to locate the explicit prediction each viewpoint makes. A prediction is a testable statement about what should happen to a measurable variable (the outcome) under specific conditions. Support is found when the observed data aligns with a viewpoint's predicted direction (e.g., an increase vs. a decrease) and magnitude (the size of the change).

sections.title: Evaluating Controls and Alternatives
sections.content: A result that matches a prediction is only strong evidence if the experiment was designed to rule out other causes. Viewpoints often disagree because one scientist believes a specific 'confounding variable' (like light, temperature, or pressure) is the real cause of an effect. To support one viewpoint over another, the experiment must control for the alternative explanation proposed by the opposing side. If the alternative explanation was not controlled, the results may be considered inconclusive.

sections.title: The Support Checklist
sections.content:
To decide which viewpoint is supported, follow these steps: 1. Identify the numeric or directional prediction for each viewpoint. 2. Compare the new data to these predictions. 3. Check if the experiment controlled for the variables mentioned in the opposing viewpoint. 4. Select the viewpoint that matches the data and whose alternatives were ruled out.

![A flowchart showing the steps to evaluate if new evidence supports a scientific viewpoint.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/2a426a9f-6aa3-4a9c-bed9-2fdc08a808c3-1786506730662-917.webp)

worked_examples.question:
Context: Scientists are debating why a specific plant species grows taller in Valley A than in Valley B. 
Viewpoint 1: Soil nitrogen levels in Valley A are higher, predicting a 15-25% increase in height. 
Viewpoint 2: Differences are due to higher rainfall in Valley A, not soil quality. 
New Evidence: A study grew plants from both valleys in a greenhouse with identical water levels. Plants in Valley A soil grew 20% taller than those in Valley B soil (p < 0.05). Which viewpoint does this support?
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Identify predictions. Viewpoint 1 predicts a 15-25% height increase due to soil. 
Step 2: Compare results. The 20% increase matches Viewpoint 1's predicted magnitude and direction. 
Step 3: Evaluate controls. The greenhouse used 'identical water levels,' which controls for the rainfall variable mentioned in Viewpoint 2. 
Conclusion: The evidence supports Viewpoint 1 because the result matches its prediction and the alternative explanation (water) was ruled out.

common_mistakes: Ignoring Magnitude: Choosing a viewpoint because the direction matches, even if the size of the effect is far smaller or larger than predicted.
Overlooking Controls: Supporting a viewpoint based on a result without checking if the experiment actually ruled out the other scientist's proposed cause.
Misinterpreting 'Inconclusive': Selecting 'inconclusive' just because the data is complex, even when a clear match and control exist.
exam_tips: Look for phrases like 'identical conditions' or 'held constant' to identify which alternative explanations have been ruled out.
Statistically significant results (often indicated by low p-values) provide stronger support for a viewpoint than results that could be due to chance.
If a result contradicts the predictions of all viewpoints, look for an answer choice that states the evidence supports neither.
content.recap: To determine which viewpoint new evidence supports, match the data's direction and magnitude to the viewpoints' predictions while ensuring that the experiment's controls have eliminated the alternative explanations proposed by rivals.

knowledge_claims.content: A scientific viewpoint is a proposed explanation that makes at least one explicit, testable prediction about measurable outcomes.
Evidence supports a viewpoint when observed measurements align in both direction and plausible magnitude with that viewpoint’s prediction.
The first step in evaluating new evidence is to locate the explicit prediction each viewpoint makes about measurable outcomes.
To confirm support for a viewpoint, one must verify that the experiment controlled for the main alternative explanations named by the opposing viewpoint.
If a new result matches a viewpoint's prediction and the experiment's controls rule out the opponent's alternative explanation, that viewpoint is supported.
It is a mistake to label a result 'inconclusive' if the experiment successfully controlled for stated alternatives and produced a statistically significant match to a prediction.
Directional predictions involve statements about whether a variable will increase, decrease, or stay the same.
Magnitude predictions involve specific numeric ranges or percentages of expected change in a variable.
When two viewpoints exist, an experiment that holds one variable constant (a control) is specifically designed to test the validity of the viewpoint that emphasizes that variable.
A result is considered to support neither viewpoint if the observed data contradicts the fundamental predictions of all models presented.
When comparing results to predictions, one should note both the direction of change and the approximate size (magnitude) of the effect.
A result is inconclusive if the experimental design fails to account for a primary confounding variable proposed by a competing viewpoint.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 3: Paper Rotor Descent
A class built paper rotors with two folded blades. Experiment 1 compared blade lengths while rotor mass was held constant. Experiment 2 added paper clips to the medium-blade rotor. Students released each rotor from the same height indoors and recorded mean descent time.

Which follow-up would most directly strengthen or extend the investigation?
A) Repeat only the result that best matches the original expectation and discard the others.
B) Change every variable at once so that no control condition remains.
C) Stop collecting measurements and infer the answer from the graph title.
D) Test several intermediate blade lengths while keeping rotor mass constant.

options.A: Repeat only the result that best matches the original expectation and discard the others.
options.B: Change every variable at once so that no control condition remains.
options.C: Stop collecting measurements and infer the answer from the graph title.
options.D: Test several intermediate blade lengths while keeping rotor mass constant.

items.explanation: The proposed follow-up changes or replicates conditions in a way that produces interpretable additional evidence.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 4: Stream Turbidity After Rain
A watershed team measured turbidity at an upstream forest site and a downstream roadside site before rainfall and at three times after a storm. Higher turbidity means that more suspended particles scatter light.

Which prediction is most consistent with the pattern and appropriately qualified?
A) All future measurements must equal the last measured value exactly.
B) By 18 hours, turbidity at both sites would likely be lower than at 12 hours if the declining trend continued.
C) Changing the x-variable cannot affect the measured outcome.
D) A single plotted point proves a universal scientific law.

options.A: All future measurements must equal the last measured value exactly.
options.B: By 18 hours, turbidity at both sites would likely be lower than at 12 hours if the declining trend continued.
options.C: Changing the x-variable cannot affect the measured outcome.
options.D: A single plotted point proves a universal scientific law.

items.explanation: The prediction extends the observed pattern cautiously rather than claiming certainty.

videoLesson.title: Decide Which Viewpoint Evidence Supports
videoLesson.description: Recognize which model the new numeric result aligns with by comparing predicted outcomes and measured variables. Match predicted direction and magnitude, then check controls for key alternative explanations.
